scenes.title: Reuse an A value across columns.
Reuse a B value across rows.
Keep the sums. Replace the inputs.
Sharing belongs to an output tile.

cues.text: Matrix multiplication combines inputs with weights in a neural network. Start with the four by four matrices from Chapter Nine.
One output combines a row from matrix A with a column from matrix B. The K index selects the matching pair of inputs.
This is our teaching algorithm. PyTorch selects its own implementation for the matrix operation.
For row zero and column zero, multiply each matching pair, then add the four products. The output is one point zero.
Our first algorithm gives each output its own thread. Each thread loads both inputs for every product.
Neighbouring outputs need some of the same inputs. Could a block load those inputs once and share them?
A tile is a small rectangular part of a matrix. Choose a two by two output tile, with one output per thread in our block.
Load both input tiles into shared memory: four values from matrix A, and four from matrix B. These cover K positions zero and one.
This group of K positions is one phase. The four threads use the input tiles to build four partial sums.
Follow the highlighted value from matrix A: minus two, at row zero and K zero.
It combines with two different values from matrix B, contributing to output columns zero and one in the same row.
The block keeps the input in shared memory so both threads can use it. Our count includes both products, even when one is zero.
Now follow minus one from matrix B, at K zero and column zero.
It combines with different values from matrix A, contributing to output rows zero and one in the same column.
Each loaded value serves two outputs in this phase. The two input tiles contain eight values; separate output threads would load sixteen inputs for those same products.
We have included only the first two K positions. Each thread retains its own partial output sum while the block moves to the next phase.
The shared input tiles can be replaced only after every thread using them has finished. A real shared-memory implementation needs ordering between these uses and writes.
The new input tiles must also be ready before threads read them, applying the barrier reasoning from Chapter Eight.
The next input tiles cover K positions two and three. Their products are added to the existing partial sums.
For output row zero, column zero, the first phase contributed two. The second contributes minus one, leaving one point zero.
All four K positions are now included. This output tile matches the separate-output algorithm. The remaining output tiles follow the same pattern.
Across the complete multiplication, tile width one loads one hundred and twenty-eight input values. Width two loads sixty-four. Width four loads thirty-two.
All three algorithms produce the same sixteen output values. Larger tiles share each loaded input across more outputs in one phase.
These are explicit input-load counts. They exclude cache reuse and do not measure physical memory transactions or GPU speed.
Try eight by eight matrices with tile width four. Focus on just one output tile and one K phase.
First count the input values loaded for this phase. Then explain how one loaded input can contribute to several outputs in the tile.
Consider a different output tile elsewhere in the matrix. Can it automatically use the same load? Pause here to explain your reasoning.
The phase loads sixteen values from each input matrix: thirty-two in total. Each loaded value contributes to four outputs in this output tile.
A different output tile can load the same input again. Sharing within one block does not automatically supply another block's workspace.
Return to Chapter Nine. Change only tile width, compare the complete output and input-load counts, and explain the reuse before making any performance claim.
